newsitem.title: UK: South Africa seen as attractive long-term market.
newsitem.headline: South Africa seen as attractive long-term market.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela's positive remarks on the South African economy on Friday would add to bullish foreign investor sentiment and spur increased interest in the country from emerging market funds, analysts said.
Recent economic growth in South Africa is expected to continue and analysts said although Mandela's speech contained no hard news, it would encourage foreign investors.

Addressing the opening of the 1997 session of parliament, Mandela said the government was accelerating implementation of its macro-economic plan and said he believed the country had turned the corner towards consistent economic expansion.

Anthony Garnett of Barings told Reuters money flowing into American pension and mutual funds was looking for a home. He said South Africa could benefit while investors are currently wary of putting funds into Asia.
"Emerging market funds have low exposure to South Africa. They are very, very sensitive to changes in the mood," he said.

"His speech will do nothing to harm foreign investors, it will encourage them. The reasons are not necessarily because of the speech but because of the attitude to South African equities at this time," Garnett said.
The rand hit a low against the dollar of 4.767 in November and has since rallied almost seven percent to 4.441. Analysts see its recovery continuing.
"The market bottomed in August but it has been gaining ground since then. It's been a buy for the past five months," said Graham Bell of Standard Bank.

However Garnett was more restrained on the short-term outlook. "People have been very wary of South Africa. The local economic story is not looking great for the first half of this year...But looking ahead to 1998 economic growth will pick up."
He said personal consumption, export earnings and gross domestic fixed investment would pick up in the second half of 1997 and into 1998.
"I wouldn't commit myself to say there's a near-term story of earnings growth, but money flows will find South Africa attractive against the poor performance of last year," he said.
Another London-based analyst said South Africa had been looking a lot better in the last month.

"Since the start of year it's a much improved situation... Gilts are particularly well in demand on the strength of the rand...Emerging market money is waiting to see the GDP growth rate rise. If they can build the GDP growth rate they will expect, and will get, inward investment," he added.
The market was disappointed at the lack of specifics in Mandela's speech on the removal of foreign exchange controls and he was seen as reiterating old pledges on privatisation.
"In sentiment terms it does help, though the market was expecting more," said one analyst who declined to be named.

"(Mandela's speech) didn't contain earth-shattering news but it was part of the general improvement in climate and sentiment in South Africa which has been going on for a few months now," said Bell. He said the positive trends included a falling budget deficit, commitment to privatisation and tight monetary policy.
"I think they're following policies that are reasonably sensible," Bell said.
Mandela said the government's privatisation programme would be pushed ahead and telecommunications parastatal Telkom would acquire a strategic equity partner in a matter of months.
"On Telkom, that's a significant breakthrough," said Bell.
"South Africa is not an exciting emerging market country. It's a longer-term story and you've got to be optimistic. It's a five-year plan, not a five minute plan," the London analyst said.
